name: powerman
desc: Control (remotely and in parallel) switched power distribution units
why: Controls networked power distribution units in parallel, a quiet look at how data centres physically switch machines on and off.

brief.what_it_is: powerman is free UNIX/Linux software that controls switched power distribution units (PDUs) remotely and in parallel. It takes a set of devices and control actions (power on, off, cycle and similar) from the command line or a daemon, and sends them to the hardware over telnet, raw socket, or serial connections, or through coprocess plugins for other protocols. It gives the equipment unified names and runs control actions in parallel. The README lists executables httppower, plmpower, pm, powerman, powermand and redfishpower, but does not describe what each one does.
brief.why_it_exists: It was designed for remote power control of Linux systems in a data center or cluster environment. The README says it has also been used in embedded management appliances, home automation, and high availability service management.
brief.how_it_works: Devices are described to powerman through an expect-like scripting language, so new hardware can be supported without changing the core. Native communication uses telnet, raw socket, and serial protocols. A coprocess interface lets virtual power control devices talk other protocols, and the README names SNMP, IPMI, Insteon, and Redfish as ones it has been extended to reach.
brief.install_notes: The README does not give installation steps or runtime requirements beyond the brew install, and it does not describe first-run configuration. The executables list suggests a powermand daemon alongside client tools, but the README does not confirm how they fit together.
brief.standout: Equipment from very different control paths (telnet, serial, SNMP, IPMI, Insteon, Redfish) is driven through one unified naming and parallel-execution layer. Devices are added by writing expect-like scripts or coprocesses rather than changing the core, and the project dates to 2002 LLNL cluster work.
brief.status: unknown. The README shows no release version, last commit date, or maintenance note. The scout note calls it quiet, which is consistent with the README but is not evidence of status on its own. The license and origin note (UCRL-CODE-2002-008, SPDX GPL-2.0-or-later) is present.
brief.caveats: The README gives no build, platform, or dependency details, and no first-run guide. Commands are not shown, so usage must be taken from the docs, which I did not fetch. The brew_caveats field is empty. Licensing is GPL-2.0-or-later.

judge.reason: A niche but substantial hardware-control tool: it unifies serial and networked power devices, letting you switch machines in parallel through an extensible scripting layer.

entry.title: powerman
entry.tldr: Remote, parallel control of switched power distribution units, driven by expect-style scripts that teach it new hardware. A look at how clusters get power-cycled.
entry.deeper_look:
powerman turns a rack of switched power distribution units (PDUs) into something with names you can address. You give it devices and actions such as on, off or cycle. It sends them to the hardware in parallel over telnet, raw sockets or serial lines, or through coprocess plugins for other protocols.

It began as cluster work at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in 2002. The README says it was designed for "remote power control of Linux systems in a data center or cluster environment". It also says it has been used in embedded management appliances, home automation and high availability service management.

The idea underneath is the physical layer of operations. When a machine hangs hard, someone has to cut its power, and that someone is usually a script talking to a box with a telnet prompt. powerman hides the differences between those boxes. Each device is described in an expect-like scripting language, so new hardware can be supported without changing the core. The README says the coprocess interface has reached SNMP, IPMI, Insteon and Redfish.

The executables list suggests a `powermand` daemon with client tools such as `powerman` and `pm`, plus helpers like `httppower`, `plmpower` and `redfishpower`. The README does not say how they fit together, so check the docs before assuming.
entry.install:
brew install powerman
# Real use needs a switched PDU or another power-control device reachable over network or serial. Without one you can only read the help output.

Shows the daemon's options, which hints at how devices are configured and served.

entry.whats_unique: Telnet, serial, SNMP, IPMI, Insteon and Redfish devices all sit behind one naming and parallel-execution layer. New devices are added by writing expect-like scripts rather than changing the core.
entry.caveats: Useful only with real power-control hardware, and the README gives no first-run guide, commands or maintenance status.
